avoid.reason: The Las Tres Mil Viviendas (Polígono Sur) housing estate in the south has serious crime and no tourist sights.
Pickpockets work Santa Cruz's lanes, the cathedral area and the packed Semana Santa and Feria crowds.

hood_desc: Santa Cruz is the atmospheric old Jewish quarter, a maze of whitewashed lanes and hidden plazas beside the Cathedral and Alcazar, ideal for first-timers who want to be in the postcard heart of the old town despite the crowds and tourist prices.

Triana sits across the river and keeps a proud working-class identity with ceramics workshops, flamenco roots, a lively food market and authentic tapas bars, suiting travelers who want local color and a neighborhood feel a short walk from the center.

El Arenal stretches between the Cathedral and the river around the Maestranza bullring, a central and slightly quieter area with classic tapas taverns and riverside strolls, good for those wanting a walkable base without the deepest tourist crush.

La Macarena is a genuine residential district to the north around its famous basilica, less touristy and more affordable with a bohemian, everyday Sevillano atmosphere, best for budget-minded visitors seeking local immersion.

Alameda, centered on the leafy Alameda de Hercules, is the hip, bohemian and LGBTQ-friendly hub with vintage shops, buzzing bars and the citys best nightlife, perfect for younger travelers who want energy after dark.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout the city.

transit.pay: Use the rechargeable Tarjeta Multiviaje, a TUSSAM/Metro smartcard sold at TUSSAM offices, metro machines and some kiosks (refundable deposit); contactless bank-card tap-to-pay is not yet accepted onboard. A single paper ticket costs about €1.40 (around $1.55), the Multiviaje card lowers each ride to roughly €0.69, and a 1-day tourist pass costs €5 (about $5.50).
transit.hours: Metro trains run about 6:30am to 11pm weekdays, extending to around 1-2am on Friday, Saturday and pre-holiday nights; buses and the tram keep similar hours, with a few night ("Búho") lines on weekends.

food.name: Salmorejo
food.desc: Thick chilled cream of tomato and bread, richer than gazpacho, topped with diced jamon iberico and hard-boiled egg. A Seville summer staple.

places.name: Bodeguita Antonio Romero
places.note: Family-run tiled bar near the bullring; its salmorejo and montaditos pull a local crowd.

places.name: La Azotea
places.note: Modern tapas favourite with a silky, well-seasoned version and good wines by the glass.

places.name: Casa Morales
places.note: Bodega from 1850 with giant clay wine jars and unfussy, honest Andalusian tapas.

food.name: Espinacas con garbanzos
food.desc: Moorish-rooted stew of spinach and chickpeas with cumin, garlic and paprika, scooped up with bread. Seville's best-loved meat-free tapa.

places.name: El Rinconcillo
places.note: Seville's oldest bar, open since 1670; widely called the benchmark for this dish.

places.name: Bodega Santa Cruz Las Columnas
places.note: Standing-room institution by the cathedral with cheap tapas chalked on the wall.

places.name: Bar Alfalfa
places.note: Tiny corner bar with a tight traditional tapas list and a warm welcome.

food.name: Rabo de toro
food.desc: Oxtail braised for hours in red wine with vegetables until it slides off the bone, served with fries or potato puree.

places.name: El Rinconcillo
places.note: Fork-tender chunks in a deep wine gravy, poured alongside a chalked-on-the-bar tab.

places.name: Taberna Coloniales
places.note: Perennially packed tavern; expect a wait, but portions are generous and cheap.

places.name: Bodeguita Antonio Romero
places.note: Reviewers single out the oxtail here alongside the classic Triana-tiled setting.

food.name: Pescaito frito
food.desc: Andalusian fried fish - cazon en adobo, boquerones, chocos - in a light chickpea-flour crust, fried fast and eaten from a paper cone.

places.name: Freiduria Puerta de la Carne
places.note: Classic takeaway fry shop; order by weight and eat it on the square outside.

places.name: Bar Las Teresas
places.note: Hams hanging from the ceiling, marble counter and reliably crisp fried fish.

places.name: Freiduria Blanca Paloma
places.note: Neighbourhood favourite across the river where Sevillanos queue for Friday fry-ups.

food.name: Montadito de pringa
food.desc: Small warm roll stuffed with the shredded pork, beef and chorizo left over from a cocido stew. The classic one-bite Seville snack.

places.name: Bodega Santa Cruz Las Columnas
places.note: The pringa here is the city's most famous; eat it standing at the bar.

places.name: Casa Morales
places.note: Old-school bodega where the montaditos come with a glass of fino straight from the barrel.

places.name: Taberna Coloniales
places.note: Big-portion tapas bar with a terrace on a leafy square, popular with locals.

food.name: Solomillo al whisky
food.desc: Pork tenderloin medallions in a garlicky whisky and lemon sauce, mopped up with bread. Invented in Seville and on nearly every tapas menu.

places.name: Bodega Santa Cruz Las Columnas
places.note: Cheap, fast and buzzing; a good place to try the dish in its natural habitat.

places.name: Bodeguita Antonio Romero
places.note: Consistently well-rated for its Andalusian classics, including the whisky sauce.

places.name: Ovejas Negras
places.note: Small modern tapas bar near the cathedral that updates old Sevillano recipes.

food.name: Fino and manzanilla sherry
food.desc: Bone-dry chilled sherry from Jerez and Sanlucar, poured in small glasses and drunk with almost every tapa in the city.

places.name: Casa Morales
places.note: Sherry drawn straight from towering clay tinajas; among the most atmospheric pours in town.

places.name: El Rinconcillo
places.note: Bartenders still chalk your tab on the wooden bar as they pour the fino.

places.name: Bar Las Teresas
places.note: Century-old bar with a strong sherry list to match its jamon and fried fish.

food.name: Rebujito
food.desc: Feria favourite mixing chilled fino sherry with lemon soda over ice and mint - refreshing, low in strength and made for hot afternoons.

places.name: La Azotea
places.note: Modern tapas spot with a proper drinks programme and knowledgeable staff.

places.name: Bodega Santa Cruz Las Columnas
places.note: Order one at the bar and drink it on the street with the crowd, as locals do.

places.name: Ovejas Negras
places.note: Lively little bar on Calle Hernando Colon, good for a first drink of the evening.

landmarks: Seville Cathedral & Giralda Tower
The largest Gothic cathedral in the world houses Christopher Columbus's tomb, while its Giralda bell tower — a converted minaret — offers unforgettable panoramic views via a ramp instead of stairs.
Real Alcázar of Seville

A dazzling royal palace blending Mudéjar, Gothic, and Renaissance styles with intricate tilework and lush gardens, still used by the Spanish royal family and famed as a Game of Thrones filming location.
Plaza de España

A monumental semicircular plaza with a canal, ornate bridges, and colorful ceramic alcoves representing Spain's provinces — an architectural showstopper and one of the most photographed spots in the country.
Barrio Santa Cruz
Seville's former Jewish quarter, a maze of whitewashed alleys, flower-filled courtyards, and orange trees that epitomizes the romantic charm of old Andalusia.
Torre del Oro
This 13th-century Moorish watchtower on the banks of the Guadalquivir River once guarded the city's harbor and remains an enduring riverside icon.
Metropol Parasol (Las Setas)
A striking modern wooden lattice structure known as 'the mushrooms,' offering a rooftop walkway with sweeping views over the historic center.
Plaza de Toros de la Maestranza
One of Spain's oldest and most beautiful bullrings, an elegant white-and-ochre landmark that's central to Seville's cultural identity.
Triana Neighborhood
The vibrant birthplace of flamenco across the river, known for ceramic workshops, lively tapas bars, and an authentic slice of Sevillano life.
Casa de Pilatos
A stunning Andalusian palace blending Mudéjar and Renaissance architecture around tranquil tiled courtyards, considered a precursor to the Alcázar's style.
Puente de Triana (Isabel II Bridge)
Seville's oldest surviving bridge, a 19th-century iron structure spanning the Guadalquivir with beautiful views of the city skyline, especially at sunset.

train.note: No international trains run from Seville. Fast AVE and Avlo trains from Sevilla Santa Justa reach Madrid in about 2h30 and continue to Córdoba, Málaga, Valencia and Barcelona. For neighbouring Portugal there is no direct train - take a bus instead.

bus.note: International coaches to Portugal use Seville's Plaza de Armas bus station; the Lisbon run takes roughly 6-7 hours. ALSA and FlixBus both serve the route - carry ID, though there are no routine border checks within the Schengen area.

ferry.note: Seville is a river port with no scheduled passenger ferries. The nearest international crossings to Morocco (Tangier) leave from Tarifa, Algeciras and the Bay of Cádiz, about 1.5-2h south; Cádiz also has domestic ferries to the Canary Islands (Naviera Armas/Trasmediterranea).

half.name: Córdoba

half.name: Ronda
half.blurb: Dramatic clifftop town split by a deep gorge and spanned by an iconic stone bridge.

half.name: Cádiz
half.blurb: Ancient sea-ringed port with golden beaches, a grand cathedral and lively old-town streets.

half.name: Carmona
half.blurb: Hilltop town with Roman ruins, Moorish gates and a handsome fortified alcázar.

half.name: Itálica
half.blurb: Sprawling Roman ruins with a vast amphitheater and beautifully preserved mosaic floors.

half.name: Jerez de la Frontera
half.blurb: Sherry capital famed for its bodegas, dancing Andalusian horses and flamenco heritage.
